# HyperFund/HyperVerse: Investigative Report on Alleged Crypto-Ponzi Mechanics, Promotion, Rebranding, and the “Steven Reece Lewis” Persona

## Executive assessment

The evidence indicates that HyperFund was structured as a global cryptocurrency investment and recruitment operation that combined promised passive returns, multi-level referral incentives, internal crypto accounting units, restricted withdrawal mechanisms, and repeated rebranding. The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) alleges that the operation functioned simultaneously as a pyramid scheme and a Ponzi scheme: recruitment generated new deposits, while investor withdrawals were allegedly funded primarily by later investor money rather than by genuine cryptocurrency-mining revenue. The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) separately brought criminal charges against Sam Lee and Rodney Burton and announced Brenda Chunga’s guilty plea in connection with the alleged scheme. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases); [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The evidence also supports the conclusion that public-facing credibility was central to the recruitment strategy. Promoters highlighted Sam Lee, the HyperTech Group, purported relationships with DigitalX and IBM, alleged crypto-mining operations, celebrity endorsements, and the supposed HyperVerse chief executive “Steven Reece Lewis.” The SEC alleges that the “Steven Reece Lewis” persona was fabricated and performed by a paid actor, while The Guardian independently reported that the claimed educational and employment history could not be verified. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11); [S3](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

My assessment is that the network’s most significant vulnerability was not merely that it promised unusually high returns. It was that the business model appears to have used a coordinated legitimacy architecture—technical language, corporate affiliations, celebrity messaging, executive branding, and successive “new” projects—to sustain recruitment after withdrawal problems emerged. The available evidence strongly supports this assessment, although the criminal allegations against Lee and Burton remain allegations unless established in court. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases); [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

## Sources and evidentiary hierarchy

This report relies on three source records supplied in the case materials.

| Source ID | Source | Evidentiary significance |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | U.S. Department of Justice, “HyperFund and Associated Cases” | Official case page describing criminal charges, docket information, procedural updates, and alleged mechanics |
| S2 | U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, *SEC v. Xue Samuel Lee and Brenda Indah Chunga*, Complaint | Primary civil pleading containing detailed allegations, transaction mechanics, promotional statements, alleged losses, and legal theories |
| S3 | Sarah Martin, The Guardian, January 4, 2024 | Investigative reporting on the HyperVerse CEO persona, celebrity promotion, public claims, and investor recruitment |

S2 is the most detailed source for the alleged operational structure because it is the SEC’s filed complaint. However, it is a pleading and therefore contains allegations by the Commission rather than adjudicated findings. S1 is authoritative for the status of the federal criminal cases but likewise distinguishes charges from convictions. S3 is valuable corroborating investigative reporting, especially concerning the apparent nonexistence of the “Steven Reece Lewis” biography, but it should be read as journalism rather than a judicial finding.

## Network identity and timeline

### HyperFund, HyperVerse, and HyperNation

The SEC alleges that the operation began as HyperFund in June 2020 under the umbrella of the HyperTech Group. It was subsequently rebranded as HyperVerse in approximately December 2021 and later as HyperNation in approximately May 2022. The SEC describes the successive names as iterations of the same project rather than clearly independent enterprises. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The DOJ similarly identifies HyperFund as also known as HyperTech, HyperCapital, HyperVerse, and HyperNation. Its case page states that Lee allegedly co-founded HyperFund, while Rodney Burton and Brenda Chunga acted as promoters. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases))

The rebranding sequence appears significant for two reasons. First, it enabled the organization to replace an increasingly discredited investment narrative with new themes: decentralized finance, a metaverse, and eventually a masked decentralized-government project. Second, it provided a mechanism for continuity. According to the SEC, the transition from HyperFund to HyperVerse was largely automatic for existing investors, with investors directed to a new website after the original platform was disabled. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

### Timeline of key developments

| Period | Development | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| June 2020 | HyperFund launched by the HyperTech Group | S2 |
| June 2020–May 2022 | Membership packages and alleged return program operated | S2 |
| Fall/December 2021 | HyperFund rebranded as HyperVerse; launch event introduced “Steven Reece Lewis” | S2, S3 |
| November/December 2021 | Investors reportedly experienced withdrawal difficulties | S2 |
| February/March 2022 | SEC alleges withdrawals became unavailable | S2 |
| May 2022 | HyperVerse rebranded as HyperNation | S2 |
| June 2022 | HOO Exchange suspended withdrawals, according to the SEC complaint | S2 |
| November 2022 | HOO Exchange reportedly stopped functioning, ending practical redemption | S2 |
| January 29, 2024 | DOJ charges announced; Chunga’s plea unsealed; SEC complaint filed | S1, S2 |
| July 23, 2026 | DOJ case page records Burton’s 32-month sentence and three years of supervised release | S1 |

## Alleged Ponzi and pyramid mechanics

### Promised passive returns

The core offer was a “membership” purchased with cryptocurrency, generally Tether (USDT), at levels including $300, $500, $1,000, and $10,000. The platform represented the purchased value internally as “HyperUnits,” or HU. The SEC alleges that investors were promised passive rewards of approximately 0.5% to 1% per day, potentially reaching two or three times their initial investment. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The DOJ describes substantially the same alleged promise: returns of 0.5% to 1% daily until an investor’s original investment was doubled or tripled through supposed large-scale crypto-mining revenue. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases))

The return structure was economically implausible on its face. A daily return of 0.5% compounded over an extended period would produce an extremely high annualized result; the promotional promise of tripling an investment within 600 days was therefore a central inducement rather than a conventional investment projection. The sources do not establish that every investor received the same treatment or that all advertised returns were actually paid. They do establish that these returns were promoted as part of the membership program. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases); [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

### Recruitment-based rewards

The operation also offered “accelerated” rewards tied to recruitment. The SEC alleges that the Community Rewards program paid commissions through as many as 20 levels of a participant’s downline. VIP and Global Rewards allegedly provided additional benefits to higher-level recruiters, with the highest “VIP 5 STAR” level requiring at least $5 million in new membership sales. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

This feature supports the SEC’s characterization of the operation as pyramid-like. Investors were not only encouraged to deposit funds; they were encouraged to recruit others and reinvest their purported rewards. Reinvestment allegedly increased the internal membership balance while reducing pressure on the platform to provide immediate cash withdrawals. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The Guardian’s account independently describes a similar structure: members could earn referral commissions based on direct recruits and additional commissions on recruits several levels below them. It also reports that investors were encouraged to reinvest rather than withdraw and that earlier investors were sometimes able to make withdrawals before the system became inaccessible. ([S3](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

### Alleged Ponzi funding model

The SEC alleges that HyperFund had no meaningful source of revenue other than investor funds, did not operate the large-scale crypto-mining business used to justify the returns, and paid withdrawals with new investor deposits. That is the central allegation supporting the Ponzi characterization. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The alleged mechanics can be summarized as follows:

1. A participant purchased a membership using USDT or, in some instances, fiat currency.
2. The platform credited the participant with HyperUnits.
3. The participant was promised passive daily rewards.
4. The participant could increase potential rewards through recruitment and “rebuys.”
5. Withdrawal required conversion from HyperUnits into Molecular Future (MOF), followed by transfer through the HOO Exchange.
6. The SEC alleges that the conversion mechanism exposed investors to severe price deterioration and that MOF was worth only a small fraction of the nominal HyperUnit value by September 2023.
7. Withdrawal problems emerged, followed by platform and exchange failures.

The SEC complaint alleges that the HyperUnits appeared to be valued at $1 when deposited but were not actually pegged to $1 when converted for withdrawal. The complaint states that MOF was quoted at approximately $0.00001949 on September 4, 2023, although the SEC’s statement concerns available price data and does not establish the precise value of every investor’s account. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

## Public promoters and credibility engineering

### Brenda Chunga and U.S. recruitment

The SEC identifies Brenda Chunga, known online as “Bitcoin Beautee,” as one of the leading U.S. promoters. It alleges that she hosted online seminars, narrated promotional presentations, encouraged investors to focus on passive rewards, and promoted recruitment-based earnings. According to the complaint, she reached the VIP 5 STAR level within approximately six months and received approximately $3.7 million through platform withdrawals and direct transactions with investors. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The SEC further alleges that Chunga withdrew approximately $2.5 million from the platform and received approximately $1.1 million directly from investors, including fees for transferring Tether or HyperUnits. It alleges that she used the proceeds for luxury expenditures, including property, vehicles, jewelry, clothing, and recruitment events. These are allegations in the SEC complaint, not independent findings of criminal liability. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

Chunga pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit securities fraud and wire fraud, according to DOJ. The DOJ page also states that she separately agreed to settle the SEC’s civil charges. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases))

### Sam Lee and organizational credibility

The SEC alleges that Sam Lee was centrally involved from the beginning, acted as a co-founder of HyperFund or the HyperTech Group, and was used in promotional materials as a source of credibility. The complaint states that promotional materials emphasized his media appearances, business background, and association with Blockchain Global. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The SEC also alleges that HyperFund promotional materials falsely represented affiliations with DigitalX and IBM. According to the complaint, DigitalX issued a February 2021 notice disavowing any association with HyperTech Group, HyperFund, and related projects. The complaint separately alleges that IBM was not involved with Hcash, despite promotional claims. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

These claims matter because they suggest that the recruitment strategy did not rely solely on promises of returns. It also relied on an apparent corporate network that made the project look established, technically sophisticated, and connected to recognizable institutions.

## The questionable CEO persona

### “Steven Reece Lewis”

HyperVerse introduced “Steven Reece Lewis” as its chief executive during a December 2021 launch event. Promotional materials allegedly described him as a graduate of the University of Leeds and holder of a Cambridge master’s degree, with prior work at Goldman Sachs, a sale of a web-development company to Adobe, and experience founding an information-technology startup. ([S3](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

The Guardian reported that neither university could locate records for a person by that name, that no relevant Companies House or SEC records were found, and that Adobe filings did not show the claimed acquisition. The newspaper also reported that it could not find a LinkedIn profile or meaningful online presence beyond HyperVerse promotional materials. ([S3](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

The SEC goes further, alleging that the persona was fabricated and that the individual shown in the launch video was a paid actor who worked as a television presenter in Bangkok. It also alleges that Lee knew or recklessly disregarded that the person was not the actual CEO. These allegations have not been presented here as adjudicated facts. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

### Celebrity endorsements

The Guardian reported that HyperVerse circulated video messages from Steve Wozniak, Chuck Norris, Jim Norton, and Lance Bass. The messages encouraged support for HyperVerse but did not mention investments or money. The newspaper stated that the celebrities were available through Cameo and that there was no suggestion they understood the alleged business model. ([S3](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

This distinction is important. The available evidence supports the use of celebrity-style promotional material as a credibility device, but it does not establish that the celebrities knowingly participated in fraud or understood the investment mechanics.

## Collapse and case status

The SEC alleges that withdrawal difficulties began in late 2021, became more severe in February or March 2022, and were never resolved. It states that the HOO Exchange suspended withdrawals in June 2022 and had stopped working by November 2022. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The DOJ page describes the alleged scheme as operating from June 2020 through November 2022 and states that HyperFund raised approximately $1.89 billion. The SEC complaint states that the operation raised more than $1.7 billion, while CNBC summarizes the DOJ and SEC actions using approximately $1.9 billion. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases); [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

The difference likely reflects different calculations, dates, methodologies, or rounding. It should not be treated as evidence of separate schemes. The defensible conclusion is that the agencies allege a worldwide operation involving more than $1.7 billion and approximately $1.89 billion in different official descriptions.

As of the DOJ case-page update supplied in the materials, Rodney Burton had been sentenced on July 23, 2026, to 32 months’ imprisonment with credit for time served and three years of supervised release. The DOJ page identifies Lee’s case as docket 24-CR-21 and Chunga’s as docket 24-CR-1. It also expressly reminds readers that an indictment is an allegation and that defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases))

## Contradictions and unresolved issues

1. **Amount raised:** DOJ uses approximately $1.89 billion; SEC uses more than $1.7 billion; CNBC reports approximately $1.9 billion. These figures are close but not identical and should be reported with attribution rather than harmonized into one exact number. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases); [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

2. **Withdrawal blockage date:** CNBC states that withdrawals began to be blocked in July 2021, while the SEC describes serious withdrawal problems beginning in November/December 2021 and complete inability to withdraw by February/March 2022. This may reflect stages of restriction, different platforms, or different evidentiary descriptions. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases); [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

3. **Operational period:** The SEC says membership packages operated from June 2020 through May 2022, while the DOJ describes the alleged conspiracy through November 2022. The difference may reflect the distinction between the original membership offering and the broader network’s later activity. ([S1](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases); [S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11))

4. **Lee’s role:** The SEC alleges that Lee was a founder and remained centrally involved; The Guardian reports that Lee denied being the founder or being involved in some aspects of HyperNation. The report therefore treats Lee’s precise role as contested, while noting that official allegations attribute substantial responsibility to him. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11); [S3](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

## Conclusion

The evidence presents HyperFund/HyperVerse as an alleged investment network that fused four mutually reinforcing mechanisms: high-yield passive-return promises, recruitment commissions, a crypto-based withdrawal architecture, and repeated credibility campaigns. Rebranding allowed the project to shift from decentralized finance to a metaverse and then to a masked “decentralized government” narrative without abandoning the underlying investor community. Public promoters translated the model into accessible sales presentations, while executive and celebrity personas supplied authority and social proof.

The strongest supported assessment is that the alleged fraud depended less on a single false statement than on an ecosystem of reinforcing signals: technical terminology, named corporate entities, supposed institutional affiliations, prominent personalities, referral income, and promises of effortless daily profits. Once withdrawals became difficult, those same mechanisms appear to have helped preserve confidence long enough for the project to migrate through new names. The “Steven Reece Lewis” episode is particularly significant because it illustrates how executive identity itself could be used as an investment-recruitment asset. ([S2](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11); [S3](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist))

## References

Martin, S. (2024, January 4). *Chief executive of collapsed crypto fund HyperVerse does not appear to exist*. The Guardian. [url website](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2024/jan/04/chief-executive-of-collapsed-crypto-fund-hyperverse-does-not-appear-to-exist)

U.S. Department of Justice. (2026, July 29). *HyperFund and associated cases*. [url website](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/case/hyperfund-and-associated-cases)

U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. (2024, January 29). *Complaint: SEC v. Xue Samuel Lee and Brenda Indah Chunga, Civil Action No. 24-cv-00296*. [url website](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2024-11)
